description:
Camille Ann Brewer lives and works in the City of Detroit, Michigan.  Through the process of textile construction, Brewer’s artwork intersects cartographic and photographic images that speak to specific spaces and time. Weaving together of physical place, memory with time is the core subject of this body of work.  

The artwork is built with time-period paper maps, which illustrate spatial geography and political territory; along with paper-collaged images of people, places and things, which tie directly to the history and human relationships in space.  In patterns that support the artwork’s theme, the two disparate paper elements are then woven together to create a serendipitous making and aesthetic experience.

event_title: CCPS Photo Exhibition. This is the Place
combined_title: CCPS Photo Exhibition. This is the Place: Anna Liminowicz, Photographer
description:
There are nearly one million refugees currently living in Poland. While the vast majority arrived from Ukraine, Poland has also welcomed forcibly displaced people from Central Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East. While refugees may be different, they all search for a place that reminds them of home.
In *This Is The Place*, a project supported by the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), Anna Liminowicz asked refugees to show what, in Poland, reminds them of their home. These portraits and the personalized confessions her subjects handwrote in their native languages tell poignant stories about safety and hope.
Anna Liminowicz is an award-winning photographer and reportage journalist based in Warsaw, Poland. A frequent contributor to the *The New York Times*, *The Guardian*, *The Wall Street Journal*, *The Washington Post*, *El Pais*, *Der Spiegel* and UNHCR, Liminowicz divides her time  between assignments and long-term personal projects, mainly focusing on social issues like identity and loss, and what uplifts her subjects. She has covered the war in Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and received the 2022 Grand Press Photo Award for her project “Too Precious to Leave Behind”.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Lila Kadaj Exhibition: Tic Tic
description:
Lila Kadaj received her MFA from Wayne State University. Her work has been shown at numerous institutions, including the Detroit Institute of Arts, the Cranbrook Art Museum, and the Arab American National Museum.  She spent nearly 27 years teaching art at Detroit Public schools.

Artist statement: “When looking at a beautiful flower.  It’s just itself.  Just there......no .....it does not proclaim its purpose for blooming is to make people happy. It just is. Like standing in front of an easel and painting........just is.......no matter......what proclamations may be concluded to sway the viewer. Same thing goes for fine art.  It’s not about I am a woman....it’s not about I am a first generation Arab American.....it’s not about being a child of trauma....it’s not about a member of my family being gunned down on the street....it’s about being born a painter.....standing in front of my easel and working to create a "Piece of Fine Art". Not standing on some soap box and expecting my words to somehow qualify my painting. It’s the painting, drawing or sculpture that must speak on its own.......on how the artist......via the intellect and muse uses the elements to create something distinct and first rate.   It can be quiet or loud. I see so much very weak work uplifted not for its quality but because it’s in fashion.”

event_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
combined_title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
description:
Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union.

Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky  portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration.  

“For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.”
— Galina Lembersky, daughter

Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director.

Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky.

combined_title: Black Birth Joy: Announcing Lane Hall’s Fall Exhibition
description:
Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. 
 
Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. 

The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story.

The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan.

Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

combined_title: Grand Vision: An exhibition by Olayami Dabls
description:
Visiting artist Olayami Dabls is a storyteller, curator, educator, and mentor. He is the founder of the MBAD African Bead Museum in Detroit. Through material culture, Dabls presents commentary on the past, present, and future from African and African-American perspectives, with the understanding that generations of African ancestors used visual materials to convey information about their identity as well as send messages for healing and protection. Dabls is a luminary; for decades he has re-imagined what a museum space can be, accessible to everyone, free from the underpinnings of colonialism and the Western, often white, frame. *Grand Vision* includes a conceptual installation in the Gallery, presenting Dabls’s own work in visual conversation with African beads and artifacts from Dabls’s Bead Museum collections. 

Additionally, Dabls’s iconic outdoor sculpture *Iron Teaching Rocks Table Manners* will be installed on the U-M campus grounds near UMMA, at the intersection of State Street and South University from September 17- October 11, 2026. The project’s range intends to more fully articulate the many facets of Dabls’ creative practice, and the overlay of art, history, identity, community, and healing.

combined_title: Jada Langston Dissertation Defense: Lake Erie Hydrology Over the last 15 ka: Insights from Stable isotope Geochemistry, Water Balance Modeling and Bulk Geochemistry
event_subtitle: Lake Erie Hydrology Over the last 15 ka: Insights from Stable isotope Geochemistry, Water Balance Modeling and Bulk Geochemistry
description:
Sedimentary archives in lakes have been crucial for reconstructing climatic and hydrologic conditions of Earth’s past. The oxygen isotope records from skeletal materials are a key part of the toolkit for studying past climate with extensive use in marine and terrestrial settings including in lakes. For the Laurentide Great Lakes in North America, δ18O values (δ18Ocarb) of molluscs and ostracods (biogenic carbonates) have helped us understand their formation following the melting of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, subsequent isostatic rebound, and regional climate change over the past 15 ka. Biogenic carbonate δ18Ocarb values from Lake Erie, the shallowest of the Laurentide Great Lakes, have been critical for understanding its water balance, which is very sensitive to hydroclimate fluctuations. This works because δ18Ocarb values reflect the isotopic composition of lake water (δ18Olw), which is very sensitive to changes in lake evaporation or input sources. However, δ18Ocarb is a function of multiple hydrologic (temperature, humidity, evaporation, input sources) and isotopic levers (the isotopic composition of lake and atmosphere) which can significantly impact the δ18Ocarb value. In this dissertation, I demonstrate the advantages of evaluating the δ18Ocarb data in relation to regional water balance, lake configuration, and temperature constraints over the last 15 ka. 

Chapter 2 characterizes the modern hydrological conditions of Lake Erie by evaluating the seasonal and temporal isotopic (δ18Olw, δ2Hlw, and δ’17Olw) variability of local precipitation, river, and lake water within the lake basin. Our results show a systematic variation in δ18Olwr, d-excess and Δ17Owater data of lake waters in relation to seasonal conditions and basin location. I then utilize the well-monitored hydrological system of the Great Lakes to constrain the fraction of moisture from the lake (f) parameter and the ratio of turbulent to diffusive fractionation (phi or n) parameter for Lake Erie. Both parameters are essential to the lake-water isotope mass balance models and significantly affect the isotopic composition of the water (δ18Owater) but are poorly constrained. I show initial studies constraints on f and phi are too restricted and I proposed an updated look at the variation in f and phi values.

Chapter 3 employs the isotope mass balance framework established in Chapter 2 for paleohydrology reconstructions of Lake Erie. I utilize biogenic carbonates from sediment cores from the eastern and western basin of Lake Erie to reconstruct the isotopic composition of formation water (δ18Ofw) in respect to changing lake configurations and temperatures over the last 15ka. This chapter reviews previous assumptions about lake hydrology in relation to input sources, lake evaporation, and basin dynamics and suggests that a water balance modeling approach can be used as an additional measure to constrain lake conditions. I demonstrate with mass balance modeling that Lake Erie was an evaporative lake during from ~15 to 10 ka, contrary to previous interpretations that Lake Erie was a high stand lake. After 10 ka, our mass balance approach supports previous interpretations suggesting that Lake Erie transitioned to a highly evaporative closed basin lake before shifting to its modern hydrology ~5ka. 

Chapter 4 seeks to utilize micrite samples from the same sediment cores in Chapter 3 to evaluate whether lake micrite can reconstruct regional paleoclimate. Using x-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and clumped isotope geochemistry (Δ47), I analyzed samples for detrital contamination and whether these samples can be used to contextualize regional landscape changes in the Lake Erie basin. I find that all samples from the eastern and central basin have detrital contamination with reconstructed Δ47 temperatures ranging between 45 to 64°C. No micrite Δ47 temperature matches modern lake temperatures but matches previous Paleozoic and Mesozoic detrital limestone clasts Δ47 temperatures. 

This dissertation represents a more extensive application of water balance modeling for paleoclimate applications and contributes abundant isotopic (δ18Olw, δ2Hlw, δ’17Olw, δ18Ocarb, δ13Ccarb, and Δ47) data for modern and paleo-lake systems. The data from this dissertation illuminates a strong connection between the water balance of Lake Erie, lake evaporation, and the Laurentide ice sheet both in the modern lake and paleohydrology.

event_title: The Greek Manuscripts of the University of Michigan: A Celebration of the Collection and Its Catalogue
combined_title: The Greek Manuscripts of the University of Michigan: A Celebration of the Collection and Its Catalogue
description:
Join us to celebrate the culmination of a decade-and-a-half-long project to fully catalog the University of Michigan Library’s extraordinary collection of Greek manuscripts. 

A Catalogue of Greek Manuscripts, Volume 2 (https://myumi.ch/NXVQr), published by U-M Press, brings this monumental undertaking to a close, making one of the most extensive collections of Greek manuscripts in North America accessible to scholars around the world.

Enjoy breakfast refreshments while three scholars offer complementary perspectives on the study of Greek manuscripts:

THE MAKING OF A CATALOGUE OF GREEK MANUSCRIPTS AT THE UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN: CHALLENGES, ACHIEVEMENT, AND DISCOVERIES with Nadezhda Kavrus-Hoffmann, cataloger of U-M’s Greek manuscript collection.

Volume 2 covers eighty-four manuscripts and fragments. Overall, these manuscripts span a thousand years of history, from the ninth to the nineteenth century, and include a wide range of subjects, from Bible texts and saints' lives to church music and secular writing.

Learn about the detective work behind the project, including three especially exciting finds: a small fragment that turned out to preserve lost portions of a medieval Byzantine text on Indian mathematics; a beautifully illuminated fourteenth-century manuscript paired with poetry written specifically for it; and a manuscript that may be traced back to the personal library of a nineteenth-century monk-scholar, opening a new mystery about how it came to Michigan.

THE PRINCESS AND THE PHILOSOPHER: ANNA COMNENA AND THE MANUSCRIPTS OF ARISTOTLE'S "ETHICS" with Richard Janko, professor of Greek in the Department of Classical Studies, who has drawn on the collection for teaching and research.

The Byzantine historian and would-be empress Anna Comnena, confined for life to a nunnery in Constantinople after trying to depose her imperial brother, was a passionate philosopher. Beginning in 1118 C.E. she organized a scholarly edition of Aristotle's "Nicomachean Ethics" and induced three other scholars to write commentaries on it. Several remarkable paper manuscripts, now precisely datable because they belong to her project, reflect this effort. They show how her team evolved useful conventions like the comma and the footnote-number, and worked with Italian scholars to create the earliest translation of this work into Latin. 

ALWAYS INTERESTING: SELECTED BINDINGS FROM THE UM GREEK MANUSCRIPT COLLECTION with Julia Miller, bookbinding historian and contributor to the catalogue.

Miller will focus on a selection of bindings, looking at their structure, materials, and decoration — chosen based on gorgeous images in the catalogue of bindings ranging from small and exquisite, Mich. Ms. 68 (15th century), and larger but equally beautiful, Mich. Ms. 172 (14th century), both in their original and completely traditional Greek bindings, to the fascinating layers of repair and rebinding represented by Mich. Ms. 76 (17th century).

event_title: Collaborative Intelligence: Learning Together from Heterogeneous Data and Language
combined_title: Collaborative Intelligence: Learning Together from Heterogeneous Data and Language: Raed Al Kontar
description: Data are increasingly generated by many connected users, machines, and systems, which has led to explosive interest in collaborative analytics, such as federated learning, that borrow strength across diverse sources. To date, these efforts have focused mainly on predictive modeling. In this talk, I argue that collaboration, without untangling the nature of heterogeneity across users, can lead to swift and evident failures. Indeed, borrowing from the wrong sources can be worse than not collaborating at all. To this end, I present two frameworks that address two questions at the heart of collaboration: what to share, and whom to borrow from. First, we introduce Personalized PCA, a descriptive framework that extracts interpretable and identifiable features describing what is shared and what is unique across diverse datasets. Second, I bring language into the collaboration. When a new user has too little data to tell which collaborators are relevant, expert textual descriptions of the new system, often available yet overlooked, can fill the gap. Here, a large language model translates these descriptions into a prior over source relevance that guides learning when data are scarce and is gradually corrected as data accumulate. I conclude by highlighting future directions at the intersection of agentic AI, statistics, and decision making.

description:
Zell Visiting Writers Series craft lecutures are free and open to the public and will be offered both virtually (via Zoom) and in person (Michigan League, Henderson Room 3rd floor). Seats are offered on a first come, first served basis; please arrive early to secure a spot. Login here (no pre-registration needed): https://myumi.ch/ZellWriters26

Tisa Bryant’s writing explores Black women’s subjectivity by remixing rhetorical, literary, cinematic and visual arts techniques into original modes of narrative and storytelling.  Her latest book, *Residual*, is an assemblage of the interiors of grief, the home as archive, and the mystery of mothers, published by Nightboat Books in 2026. Her first book, *Unexplained Presence*, on the mythologies of Black presences in the arts, was reissued by Wave Books in 2024. In her afterword to *Unexplained Presence*, renowned critic Margo Jefferson hailed Tisa as a “literary and film auteur, an auteur of performance on the page, stage and screen or canvas.” 

A Boston native, Tisa was a member of the Dark Room Collective, an African-diasporic writing group that hosted a celebrated reading series in Cambridge and Boston.  She is co-editor of the three-volume, cross-referenced literary journal, *The Encyclopedia Project*, and collaborated from 2015-2018 with critic and writer Ernest Hardy on *The Black Book*, an original talk and film series presented at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles. Tisa is editor of *Deep West Assembly*, a monograph of recent works by the award-winning visual artist Cauleen Smith, forthcoming in 2026 from Astrup Fearnley Museet and Kestner Gesellschaft. She lives in Iowa City, where she is Associate Professor of English in the Nonfiction Writing Program at the University of Iowa, and is currently at work on a novel.

event_title: Double Duty: A Subsidy Design for\\Quality Promotion and Price Discipline
combined_title: Double Duty: A Subsidy Design for\\Quality Promotion and Price Discipline: Ying Fan, University of Michigan
description: This paper studies how the design of quality-linked subsidies shapes firm behavior in both quality choices and pricing decisions. We examine a major reform in Medicare Advantage that links subsidies to quality through two distinct policy parameters. We develop and estimate a structural model of demand and firm behavior to evaluate the reform, decompose its effects, and compare alternative quality-linked subsidy designs. A central finding is that a subsidy design that links product quality to both the subsidy level and the pass-through from firm prices to subsidized consumer prices can simultaneously raise quality and lower prices.

event_title: Accessible Field Paleontology: Building Community through Universal Design in the Field
combined_title: Accessible Field Paleontology: Building Community through Universal Design in the Field: Tara Lepore
description:
Accessible Field Paleontology: Building Community through Universal Design in the Field
Taormina (Tara) Lepore, Ph.D.
Assistant Professor
Mallinson Institute for Science Education
Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences
Western Michigan University
Friday, Oct. 23, 2026 - University of Michigan Paleontology Seminar

Field paleontology is a standout experience in the training and education of many paleontologists. It is to our benefit to build accessible, welcoming field paleontology experiences so all may learn and thrive in the field. Disabled people in particular face barriers to full, equitable field participation, but efforts have been made to create and assess disability accessible field experiences in geology and other field sciences. Field paleontology is one area where the science education and accessibility literature as well as practical availability of accessible field work is less widely reported. In this talk, I encourage our community to ask: What can we do, as paleontologists, to be at the forefront of accessible and equitable field experiences for all?

As a paleontologist and a discipline-based geoscience education researcher, I will discuss my path in science and the rationale for this type of work. A brief overview of the relevant accessible science education and outreach literature on accessible field work will be discussed, as well as current research efforts to build affirming classroom and field environments that utilize Universal Design and the theoretical frameworks of humanizing STEM and culturally relevant pedagogy, all with a disability focus. Finally, this talk will highlight a recent accessible field paleontology experience in the metro Denver area at the annual meeting of the Geological Society of America, where field participants engaged in both the local paleontology and in accessible pedagogy, and the access needs of all participants were considered at the forefront. Universal Design and the related theoretical frameworks can help us consider everyone who is present in a field paleontology experience, and can truly lead to a more accessible, inclusive, and thriving paleontological community at large.

event_title: Fore-Site (Phase 3): The Stamps Gallery Pillar Project
combined_title: Fore-Site (Phase 3): The Stamps Gallery Pillar Project
description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)
Phase 3 (September 11 - December 11) artists: Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20) and Nathan Byrne (MFA ’21)
Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. combined_title: Reverie: The Student-led Exhibition Committee Fall 2026 Exhibition
description:
A reverie is a state between waking and dreaming, a moment when the mind drifts beyond the immediate. It is a space where memory, imagination, desire, and reality can overlap, distort, and take on new forms. In these moments, the familiar can become strange, and the ordinary can become something unexpected.

Reverie brings together student works that explore the space between what is known and what is felt. Across painting, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, animation, and mixed media, the artists move through imagined landscapes, intimate encounters, memories, figures, and fragments of the everyday. These works blur the boundaries between observation and imagination, allowing emotion and perception to reshape what we recognize.

Rather than depicting dreams literally, Reverie considers dreaming as a way of seeing. The works reflect moments of escape, introspection, fantasy, and transformation, where the subconscious can surface and reality becomes open to interpretation. 

Reverie was conceived and curated by members of the Student-led Exhibition Committee (SEC), and features work by eight SEC members at the Stamps School of Art & Design. The exhibition includes ten works across oil on canvas, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, digital animation, and mixed media.

event_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

event_title: The Human Odyssey on the Roof of the World: Adaptations and Resilience on the Tibetan Plateau
combined_title: The Human Odyssey on the Roof of the World: Adaptations and Resilience on the Tibetan Plateau: Dr. Yuchao Zhao, Assistant Curator of East Asian Anthropology,  Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago
event_subtitle: Dr. Yuchao Zhao, Assistant Curator of East Asian Anthropology,  Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago
description: The Tibetan Plateau—often described as the “Roof of the World”—represents one of the most extreme environments ever inhabited by humans. With an average elevation exceeding 4000 meters, the region poses formidable challenges including hypoxia, harsh climate, and highly variable ecological productivity. Understanding how and when humans successfully adapted to these conditions remains a central question in high-altitude archaeology. This talk synthesizes recent archaeological, paleoenvironmental, and genetic research to reassess the long-term history of human occupation on the Tibetan Plateau. Evidence from Paleolithic sites indicates that foraging populations began exploring the plateau margins as early as the Middle Pleistocene, with increasing evidence for sustained human presence during the Late Pleistocene and early Holocene. Rather than viewing the plateau as permanently settled only after the arrival of agriculture and pastoralism, new research suggests that indigenous foragers played a crucial role in establishing viable lifeways in high-altitude environments.

event_title: Online Learning and Decision-Making for Dynamic Pricing and Performative Prediction
combined_title: Online Learning and Decision-Making for Dynamic Pricing and Performative Prediction: Daniele Bracale
description:
Many modern decision systems are not passive observers of the world they measure: the decisions they make change the data they subsequently receive. For example, a seller that posts a price influences the decisions of potential buyers, and hence the sales data it goes on to col-
lect; a lender that deploys a credit-scoring rule changes the nature of the loan applications it receives. In such settings, the classical separation
between estimation and decision-making breaks down, and statistical guarantees must be derived jointly with the policy that generates the
data. This dissertation develops estimation theory and online algorithms for two such feedback settings --- dynamic pricing and performative
prediction --- with a unifying theme: shape-constrained and microfounded structure can replace the tuning parameters, smoothness assump-
tions, and parametric models on which existing methods rely.
The first part concerns dynamic pricing. We first consider a monopolistic setting with censored demand, in which the seller posts a price and
observes only whether a sale occurred. In the linear valuation model, the customer’s valuation is linear in the features of the item offered,
up to market noise with unknown distribution F. Existing methods estimate F by kernel smoothing, bandit techniques, or upper confidence
bounds; all of them impose Lipschitz or stronger conditions on F, and all of them leave the analyst to choose bandwidths, confidence widths,
or regularization parameters. We instead exploit the fact that F is monotone and estimate it by isotonic regression. The resulting policy car-
ries no tuning parameters whatsoever, assumes only that F is Hölder continuous, and attains sublinear regret. It also outperforms existing
methods in simulations and on transaction data from Welltower Inc. We then move to a competitive setting in which N sellers post prices
over T periods, and each seller’s demand follows a single-index model with an unknown monotone, s-concave link. We prove existence and
uniqueness of the Nash equilibrium, and give a semiparametric least-squares policy under which prices converge to the Nash equilibrium,
while each seller incurs sublinear regret.
The second part concerns performative prediction, which involves a learner and a population of agents whose actions follow a distribution
P. The learner deploys a model M that shifts this distribution from P to P(M), thereby changing the data the learner observes; the map P(M)
is called the distribution map. Much of the literature assumes that the distribution map is known, whereas we learn it from agent-response
data. We study two settings: a discrete-action framework, in which agents choose from a finite set of alternatives, and a continuous-action
framework, in which an action may be any real number. For discrete actions, we give a nonparametric estimator of the distribution map
together with an exploration--exploitation scheme that we show to be effective in minimizing the performative risk. For continuous actions,
we model agents’ responses as a cost-adjusted utility maximization problem and propose an estimator of the cost. Our approach leverages
optimal transport to align the pre-deployment distribution P with the post-deployment distribution P(M). We provide a rate of convergence
for the proposed estimator and assess its quality through empirical demonstrations on a credit-scoring dataset.

event_title: AIM Seminar: How voting goes wrong, and how it can go right: the evolution of collective intelligence
combined_title: AIM Seminar: How voting goes wrong, and how it can go right: the evolution of collective intelligence: Joshua B. Plotkin (University of Pennsylvania)
description:
Abstract: Voting sometimes works well. A crowd's average guess is often better than any individual guess. But voting can also fail, producing a biased outcome or no decision at all. I will discuss natural mechanisms that cause each of these outcomes, in groups whose members observe other voters and learn by imitating one another.

I will first describe a voter game, played online by 2,520 people, in which two parties of equal size compete to reach a supermajority. The structure of who sees whose voting intentions, which we call information gerrymandering, can bias the outcome toward one party, even when both parties are the same size and every player has the same influence. When members of both parties see mainly their own party's intentions, most groups end in deadlock.

I will then ask what individual reward scheme allows a population of self-interested imitators, each observing only part of a problem, to evolve accurate collective decisions. For linear prediction problems, rewarding individuals for their own accuracy eliminates the diversity of opinions a group needs. Rewarding those whose opinions reduce the collective error provably increases accuracy, until the group predicts perfectly. For more realistic non-linear decisions, a single majority vote cannot produce accurate decisions under any reward scheme. Voting in layers, with rewards paid only to individuals who are pivotal at every layer above them, provably allows a population to evolve accurate decisions. The evolved population is equivalent to a multi-layer perceptron in machine learning, and the reward for pivotality corresponds to credit assignment that machines compute through backpropagation. These results therefore provide a naturalistic, evolutionary account of collective in intelligence in humans and machines.

Contact: Naoki Masuda

event_title: HET Seminar | Dark Energy and Time Reparametrizations
combined_title: HET Seminar | Dark Energy and Time Reparametrizations: Jun Nian (ICTP-AP)
description:
***Please note: Due to unforeseen circumstances, this seminar has been CANCELLED***

The cosmological constant’s quantum origin is a famous open problem in theoretical physics and cosmology. Its observed value and theoretical prediction exhibit a large 120-order discrepancy. In this talk, we first summarize the current state of research on the cosmological constant problem and review the Schwarzian theory of time reparametrizations in the literature. Inspired by an early work by Gary Gibbons and our recent attempts to solve various formidable problems (e.g., color confinement in SYM, fluid/gravity correspondence at low temperatures, etc.) via the JT gravity/Schwarzian theory duality, we apply the Schwarzian theory of time reparametrizations and its ensemble average to the cosmological constant problem and propose a new approach to resolving it. We will show that this new method, at leading order, yields a theoretical value that exactly matches the observed value of the cosmological constant. However, recent results from dark energy observations (such as DESI) suggest a dynamical dark energy. Starting from the leading-order constant value, we will take into account matter-gravity interactions and develop a more realistic dynamical dark energy model based on time reparametrizations that can fit observational data with comparable precision to other models (e.g., LCDM and CPL). We also provide some falsifiable predictions for future more precise observations. This talk is based on my recent paper arXiv:2602.17476 and another upcoming work.

Brief Biography:
Jun Nian is an assistant professor at the International Centre for Theoretical Physics Asia-Pacific (ICTP-AP), University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. He received a Diplom degree from the University of Heidelberg in 2009 and a Ph.D. degree from Stony Brook University in 2015. Before joining ICTP-AP in 2021, he was a postdoctoral fellow at Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques (IHES), the University of Michigan, and the University of Milan. His research interests include quantum field theory, gravity theory, and string theory, with a recent focus on the quantum-gravitational effects in black holes and cosmology.

combined_title: Unexpected torus action on toric Richardson varieties: Soyeon Kim (UC Davis)
description: This talk focuses on Richardson varieties in the complete flag variety, which are intersections of a Schubert variety with an opposite Schubert variety. Richardson varieties are indexed by intervals in the Bruhat order on the symmetric group. In joint work with E. Gorsky and M. Sherman-Bennett, we study the following question: when is a Richardson variety a toric variety? All Richardson varieties admit an action by an (n-1)- dimensional torus in SL_n, called the standard torus, which also acts on the complete flag variety. The Richardson varieties which are toric varieties with respect to the standard torus were classified independently by Anderson and Tsukerman--Williams. We found that there are many additional toric Richardson varieties, which we call "unexpected”. In this rather expository talk, I will classify toric Richardson varieties using the combinatorics of Bruhat intervals and focus on describing this "unexpected" torus action using the Marsh--Rietsch parametrization on open Richardson varieties. If time permits, I will mention my ongoing research in this direction.

combined_title: Smith Lecture: Qinya Liu: High-resolution full-waveform seismic imaging beneath seismic arrays based on ambient-noise and teleseismic body waves
event_subtitle: High-resolution full-waveform seismic imaging beneath seismic arrays based on ambient-noise and teleseismic body waves
description: The field of seismic imaging has witnessed significant advances in the past two decades resulting from the combined improvement in observational and computational seismology, including 1) increased deployment of broadband regional seismic arrays, including dense linear arrays, 2) the use of innovative dataset such as ambient-noise cross-correlation functions and teleseismic scattered and converted waves. 3) full numerical simulations of seismic wave propagations at local, regional and global scales, and their applications to full-waveform inversions resulting in unprecedented high-resolution images of tectonic regions around the globe. To take full advantage of the dense seismic arrays, particularly for regions lacking seismicity, both ambient-noise data and teleseismic body waves can be inverted in the framework of full-waveform inversion (FWI). In this talk, I review the basic theory of utilizing these two dataset jointly in FWI, as well as in combination with local earthquake data, and show our recent lithospheric imaging applications beneath Alaska, and central Cascadia. The use of these innovative datasets in FWI provides complementary sensitivities, generates high-resolution images of the lithosphere, and hence contributes to improving their tectonic interpretations.

event_title: In the Shadow of Empire:  Calcutta’s Victoria Memorial and its Cast of Moving Statuary
combined_title: In the Shadow of Empire:  Calcutta’s Victoria Memorial and its Cast of Moving Statuary: Tapati Guha-Thakurta
description:
With a focus on Calcutta’s landmark monument – the most grandiose of the memorials to the Queen of all the ones built across the British imperial territories – this lecture addresses the theme of the end of empire through the persistence and proliferation of the genre of civic public statuary, its shifting cast of characters, and its movements across time and space. It is on the grounds of the Victoria Memorial – in the lingering shadows of a bygone empire – that a brood of imperial statues have found a safe haven, quietly living out their post-imperial lives of oblivion in a time and place where the empire is long gone but its hauntings remain.  

In the recent past, we have seen how such hauntings of the past can suddenly return to a body of long-standing statues of American Confederate leaders, slave owners and imperialists, bringing on them the wrath of anti-white supremacist protests that began to rage across Western cities and universities during 2020. What the Black Lives Matter movement did was to return attention in India to the long-forgotten specimens of colonial statuary, mostly hidden away in remote locations of our cities - raising the issue again, after over 75 years of Independence, of their rights to remain in the spaces where they still stand. The afterlives of these relics of empire is a central theme of this lecture, as it explores various moments in the travels, dislocations and relocations of Calcutta’s imperial statues, while charting a small parallel history of Indian statue-making over these transitional decades of the last years of British rule and the coming of Independence.

Tapati Guha-Thakurta was educated at Presidency College, Calcutta University, and the University of Oxford. She is currently an Honorary Professor of History at the Centre for Studies in Social Sciences, Calcutta (CSSSC) and was its former Director from 2012 to 2017. She has written widely on the art and cultural history of modern India, and has held several visiting fellowships abroad. Her three main books are The Making of a New ‘Indian’ Art: Artists, Aesthetics and Nationalism in Bengal (Cambridge University Press, 1992) and Monuments, Objects, Histories: Institutions of Art in Colonial and Postcolonial India (Columbia University Press, and Permanent Black, 2004), and In the Name of the Goddess: The Durga Pujas of Contemporary Kolkata (Delhi: Primus Books, 2015). She has also had a parallel career as exhibition curator and archivist, and has helped build a large digital image archive on the visual cultures of modern and contemporary Bengal at the CSSSC. She has co-edited three anthologies of essays – Theorising the Present: Essays for Partha Chatterjee (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2011); New Cultural Histories of India: Materiality and Practices (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2013); and How Secular is Art? On the Politics of Art, History and Religion in South Asia (Cambridge University Press, 2023). Among her other professional work is the preparation of a dossier on the Durga Pujas of Kolkata for the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, which has brought to the festival the coveted UNESCO inscription under its List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2021.

description: Engendering Respectful Communities (ERC) is a one session workshop that engages graduate students in meaningful dialogue about various forms of sexual misconduct they may encounter in both professional and social spaces, and provides resources for intervention or support in such circumstances.The primary goal of the workshop is to address complexities experienced by graduate students as they engage in bystander intervention, so that participants gain an increase in awareness of barriers to action and familiarity with strategic planning to overcome them. The workshop also introduces participants to on-campus resources and provides knowledge on how sexual misconduct can unfold in graduate-specific settings.The ERC workshop uses small-group circles intended to promote active reflection and space to build community. The procedure of circles is introduced at the beginning of the workshop in order to help participants get used to the process, which they do through a circle for introductions and value-sharing for the workshop space. These circles depict various, realistic scenarios related to sexual misconduct within the graduate community. The circle process allows circle members to process the monologues, reflect on complexities with identity and power dynamics within them, name potential barriers to intervention, and think of various ways in which they might respond if faced with similar situations. The circles provide a way to foster collective building of ideas, where participants learn from one another and all input is equally valued. Participants are encouraged to share but can always pass if desired, creating an environment where participation is open but not forced. Due to the participatory nature of the workshop, if you are to arrive more than 20 minutes late, we will ask you to re-register for another workshop session.If you have any questions about or concerns with taking this workshop, or are in need of an exemption, please contact jhippe@umich.edu or fill out this form. We know some students come to campus having already experienced harm. If you have circumstances that make completing this course challenging, please reach out to the GROWE team. SAPAC GROWE provides exemptions to the ERC workshop (where requirements are set in place) on a case by case basis. The Program Manager will communicate with students requesting exemptions via email and/or meet with students via zoom meetings to discuss their need for exemptions and provide any relevant and necessary resources.

Born in Tokyo, KOTARO FUKUMA began learning piano at the age of five and has received many high awards in international competitions. At the age of 20, Kotaro won both First Prize and the Chopin Prize at the 15th Cleveland International Piano Competition. Since then his concert career has developed in over 35 countries on five continents. 

Kotaro has performed in major concert venues, including Carnegie Hall, Lincoln Center, Wigmore Hall, Berlin Philharmonie, Konzerthaus, Gewandhaus zu Leipzig, Salle Gaveau, Victoria Hall, Auditorio Nacional de Madrid, Beijing Forbidden City Concert Hall and Tokyo Suntory Hall. His performances with orchestras include the Cleveland Orchestra, Moscow Philharmonic, Israel Philharmonic, Finnish Radio Symphony, Dresden Philharmonic, Tonkünstler Orchestra, Lille National Orchestra, Japan Philharmonic and NHK Symphony Orchestra, under the direction of such conductors as Yuri Simonov, Rafael Frühbeck de Burgos, François-Xavier Roth, Dmitry Liss, Juanjo Mena, Asher Fisch, Hannu Lintu, Mihhail Gerts and Kazuki Yamada. In 2016, with 24h-notice he stepped in for Nelson Freire to perform Brahms‘ Piano concerto No.2 with the Orchestre National du Capitole de Toulouse under Tugan Sokhiev. Kotaro Fukuma has released 21 commercial CDs and has received critical acclaim in Gramophone, Diapason, American Music Records, Monde de la Musique, Classica, Piano News, BR Klassik, Classic Today, etc. His album *Fantasy – Scriabin & Rachmaninoff* (Naxos) was nominated for the International Classical Music Award 2024.

He studied music at the Conservatoire National Supérieur de Musique de Paris with B. Rigutto and M. F. Bucquet, then at the Universität der Künste Berlin with K. Hellwig and at the International Piano Academy Lake Como in Italy. He also studied with several great masters of the piano, including L. Fleisher, M. Uchida, R. Goode, A. de Larrocha, M. J. Pires and A. Ciccolini.

Since July 2020 he has also been producing a concert series “Rare Piano Music”, in which he presents colleague pianists and rare piano repertoire. Kotaro Fukuma currently lives between Berlin, Leiden and Tokyo.

combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

event_title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
combined_title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them: Exhibit
description:
Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking.

While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last.

Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

event_title: Fore-Site (Phase 3): The Stamps Gallery Pillar Project
combined_title: Fore-Site (Phase 3): The Stamps Gallery Pillar Project
description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Each space hosts dozens of artists annually for exhibitions, performances, and events, fostering experimental work and building community. For this project, Byrne, Clegg, and Narula have been commissioned to reimagine the pillars on Division Street that flank the gallery. In response, they’ve curated six artists to create new work for the pillars over three cycles:

Phase 1 (September 12 - December 12) artists: Amelia Burns (Cranbrook MFA ’23) and Erin McKenna (MFA ’20)
Phase 2 (January 12 - August 12) artists: Sally Clegg (MFA ’20) and Kim Karlsrud (MFA ’20)
Phase 3 (September 11 - December 11) artists: Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20) and Nathan Byrne (MFA ’21)
Phase 3 

Curated by Sometimes Space: Abhishek Narula (entry pillar)
Curated by CYNK Studios: Nathan Byrne (courtyard pillar)

Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. combined_title: Reverie: The Student-led Exhibition Committee Fall 2026 Exhibition
description:
A reverie is a state between waking and dreaming, a moment when the mind drifts beyond the immediate. It is a space where memory, imagination, desire, and reality can overlap, distort, and take on new forms. In these moments, the familiar can become strange, and the ordinary can become something unexpected.

Reverie brings together student works that explore the space between what is known and what is felt. Across painting, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, animation, and mixed media, the artists move through imagined landscapes, intimate encounters, memories, figures, and fragments of the everyday. These works blur the boundaries between observation and imagination, allowing emotion and perception to reshape what we recognize.

Rather than depicting dreams literally, Reverie considers dreaming as a way of seeing. The works reflect moments of escape, introspection, fantasy, and transformation, where the subconscious can surface and reality becomes open to interpretation. 

Reverie was conceived and curated by members of the Student-led Exhibition Committee (SEC), and features work by eight SEC members at the Stamps School of Art & Design. The exhibition includes ten works across oil on canvas, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, digital animation, and mixed media.

event_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
combined_title: Cosmo Whyte: Under the Quiet, Beyond the Eye
description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

More broadly, the exhibition considers how geographic boundaries, cultural identities, and inherited histories remain fluid and contested, tracing the ways race, class, migration, and displacement shape belonging across generations.

Tours are guided by Amanda D. King, a visual artist working across image-making, social practice, and curation, and an MFA candidate at the Stamps School of Art & Design.

Free and open to the public. Registration requested.

Program will repeat on October 10 and October 24.

description:
As part of the leadup to our 150th season in 28/29, UMS is commissioning several new works across artistic disciplines. The first of these features a new, full-length dance collaboration with New York City Ballet principal dancer Sara Mearns and co-choreographers and dancers Bobbi Jene Smith and Or Schraiber, whose Obsidian was performed by Ballet BC last season.

This new piece, titled The Rose Sonata, was developed on the U-M campus in June 2026. Featuring two pianists and six dancers, the new work receives its world premiere at the Power Center in October. Smith and Schraiber started their careers as dancers with the Batsheva Dance Company and now return as world-renowned creators whose choreography has been commissioned by The Paris Opera Ballet, Royal Danish Ballet, National Ballet of Canada, and Martha Graham Dance Company, to name just a few.

Their collaborative approach to dance theater results in a stunning new ensemble work that features New York City Ballet principal dancer Sara Mearns. Mearns began studying dance at age 13 in South Carolina and entered the School of American Ballet, the official school of New York City Ballet, in 2001. She has been a principal dancer with the company since 2008.

Critics often draw comparisons between The Tallest Man on Earth and Bob Dylan, citing similarities in both songwriting and vocal style. Matsson himself has acknowledged Dylan's influence, revealing that he started listening to him at the age of fifteen. Fascinated by Dylan's covers, he delved into their origins, which gradually introduced him to early American folk artists like Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie. However, Matsson is quick to distance himself from being part of any specific tradition, stating, “I don’t want to be part of a tradition. I just want to do what feels natural to me. combined_title: Comics Beyond Sight
description:
This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. 

Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. 

Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening.

View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

combined_title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them: Exhibit
description:
Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking.

While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last.

Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

event_title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
combined_title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s: American Home Cooking
description:
Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically  grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.
